explanation_text: We are given: [latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex] Step 1: Substitute a single variable Let [latex]u = x + y[/latex] Then, the function becomes: [latex]f(x, y) = (u - 1)^2 + u^2 = u^2 - 2u + 1 + u^2 = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex] Step 2: Minimize [latex]f(u) = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex] This is a quadratic function in [latex]u[/latex] with a positive coefficient, so it has a unique minimum. The minimum occurs at: [latex]u = \frac{-(-2)}{2 \cdot 2} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] So, the function is minimized when [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] Step 3: Analyze the set [latex]S[/latex] All points [latex](x, y)[/latex] satisfying [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] will minimize [latex]f(x, y)[/latex]. [latex]f(x, y) = (u - 1)^2 + u^2 = u^2 - 2u + 1 + u^2 = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex]

All points [latex](x, y)[/latex] satisfying [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] will minimize [latex]f(x, y)[/latex].
There are infinitely many such points in [latex]\mathbb{R}^2[/latex].

[latex]\boxed{\text{The number of elements in the set } S \text{ is infinite}}[/latex]

To synchronize an alternator with the grid, the following conditions must be satisfied: The terminal voltage of the alternator should match the grid voltage. Instruments used to verify these conditions are: (A) Voltmeter:

Measures power; not used for synchronization. (C) Synchroscope:
Used to indicate the phase angle and frequency difference between the alternator and the grid. It shows whether the alternator is running fast or slow and when to close the circuit breaker. (D) Stroboscope:
Used to measure rotational speed visually; not used in electrical synchronization.

So the forward path becomes:
[latex] K(s-1)G(s) = \frac{K(s-1)}{(s+1)(s+2)} [/latex]

Step 2: Closed-loop transfer function (unity feedback):
[latex] T(s) = \frac{K(s-1)G(s)}{1 + K(s-1)G(s)} = \frac{K(s-1)}{(s+1)(s+2) + K(s-1)} [/latex]

[latex] H(j \omega)= \begin{cases}1, & |\omega| \leq 200 \pi \\ 0, & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} [/latex]

Let [latex]h(t)[/latex] be its time domain representation. Then [latex]h(0)=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Transform
explanation_html:
Step 1: Frequency response
[latex] H(j\omega) = \begin{cases} 1, & |\omega| \leq 200\pi \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} [/latex]
Step 2: Find impulse response [latex] h(t) [/latex] by inverse Fourier transform
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} H(j\omega) e^{j\omega t} d\omega [/latex]
But since [latex] H(j\omega) = 1 [/latex] for [latex] |\omega| \leq 200\pi [/latex], and 0 otherwise:
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-200\pi}^{200\pi} e^{j\omega t} d\omega [/latex]
Step 3: Evaluate the integral
This is a standard Fourier inverse transform result:
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{2 \sin(200\pi t)}{t} = \frac{200 \sin(200\pi t)}{\pi t} [/latex]
This is the sinc function scaled:
[latex] h(t) = 200 \cdot \text{sinc}(200 t) [/latex] where [latex] \text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x} [/latex]
Step 4: Find [latex] h(0) [/latex]
Use the standard limit:
[latex] \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\sin(200\pi t)}{\pi t} = 200 [/latex]
So:
[latex] h(0) = \frac{200 \sin(0)}{\pi \cdot 0} = 200 [/latex]
Final Answer: 200

Step 4: Required reactive power by capacitor bank

Step 1: Let us assume PQ = 5 units
Given the ratio [latex]PT : TR = 3 : 2[/latex], then [latex]PT = 3[/latex] units and [latex]TR = 2[/latex] units, so total [latex]PR = PT + TR = 5[/latex] units.
Since [latex]ST \parallel QR[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex] lies on [latex]PR[/latex], by Basic Proportionality Theorem:
[latex]\frac{PS}{PQ} = \frac{PT}{PR} = \frac{3}{5}[/latex]
So, [latex]PS = \frac{3}{5} \cdot PQ[/latex]

Step 2: Area of semicircle is proportional to square of diameter
Let the diameter [latex]PQ = d[/latex].
Then the area of the semicircle with diameter [latex]PQ[/latex] is:
[latex]A_{PQ} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8}[/latex]

Now, [latex]PS = \frac{3}{5} d[/latex], so area of semicircle on PS:
[latex]A_{PS} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi (3d/5)^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8} \cdot \frac{9}{25} = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}[/latex]

Step 3: Shaded Area = Area of semicircle on PQ − Area of semicircle on PS
[latex]A_{\text{shaded}} = A_{PQ} - A_{PS} = A_{PQ} \left(1 - \frac{9}{25}\right) = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}[/latex]

Now convert the shaded area as a multiple of the semicircle on PS:
[latex]\frac{A_{\text{shaded}}}{A_{PS}} = \frac{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}}{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}} = \frac{16}{9}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{\frac{16}{9}}[/latex] times the area of the semicircle with diameter [latex]PS[/latex]
